title: Beyond Epichloë: Foliar endophytic bacteria are associated with growth promotion in a grass–endophyte symbiosis
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Epichloë endophytes form stable symbioses with grasses and can exert growth-promoting effects on host plants, potentially through interactions with associated microbiomes. We compared endophyte-infected (EI) and endophyte-free (EF) Achnatherum inebrians under field conditions across four developmental stages and a maternal–offspring continuum, integrating plant growth traits with foliar bacterial community profiling. The experiment included six biological replicates for each treatment at each developmental stage. Epichloë endophyte exerted significant growth-promoting effects on both maternal and offspring A. inebrians at later developmental stages, with stronger growth-promoting effects observed in offspring plants. Amplicon sequencing revealed that plant developmental stage was the primary factor shaping foliar bacterial community structure, while Epichloë endophyte infection was associated with differences in early-stage bacterial community composition and assembly processes. These early-stage differences were accompanied by the persistent enrichment of core bacterial taxa represented by Sphingomonas during later developmental stages, increased modularity of microbial co-occurrence networks, and greater predicted functional potential related to carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Moreover, EI plants exhibited higher carbon and nitrogen contents at maturity stages, and these changes were associated with the observed growth-promoting effects, suggesting that variation in the foliar microbiome may be related to differences in host nutrient accumulation. Further culture-based isolation and inoculation experiments showed that Sphingomonas possessed multiple plant beneficial traits and exerted significant growth-promoting effects on A. inebrians at appropriate inoculation densities.
